articles.title: BLA claims 43 Pakistani personnel, ‘death squad’ members killed in Balochistan
articles.summary: Pakistan News: The Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) has claimed that 43 Pakistani military personnel and members of alleged state-backed 'death squads' were killed in 13.
articles.body: The Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) has claimed that 43 Pakistani military personnel and members of alleged state-backed 'death squads' were killed in 13 operations across Balochistan between September 7 and 13, according to a report.The Balochistan Post (TBP) said that in its weekly statement, BLA spokesperson Jeeyand Baloch said the group’s militants carried out attacks and blockades across areas including Basima, Kharan, Panjgur, Chagai, Tump, Surab, Killa Abdullah, Lasbela, Jiwani and Mashkel.The development comes as a powerful blast at a mosque inside a police compound in Kohat, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, killed at least 16 people and injured 57, police and rescue officials said on Friday. Five police officers and 11 civilians were among the dead. Seven armed gunmen also tried to enter the compound, with six killed in the ensuing gunfire.According to the BLA statement, the operations targeted military convoys, checkpoints and surveillance equipment, alongside people the BLA described as members of “death squads”. The group also reported attacks on commercial vehicles, bridges and a lithium extraction project.The claims could not be independently verified.The campaign allegedly began on September 7 with a five-hour blockade of a China-Pakistan Economic Corridor route in Basima, where the BLA said its fighters conducted checks. It claimed five Pakistani personnel were killed and several injured, while three BLA militants also died in the clashes.The following day, the group claimed an ambush on a military convoy in Kharan left at least four personnel killed or wounded. In Panjgur, it said militants attacked military supply vehicles and destroyed surveillance cameras.On September 10, the BLA claimed it blocked the Quetta-Taftan trade route in Chagai, seized two commercial vehicles and destroyed a bridge with explosives. It also claimed one of its units brought down a Pakistani military surveillance quadcopter in Tump.Two attacks were reported in Surab on September 11. The BLA claimed six military personnel were killed in an ambush on a convoy at Tobo, while another three were killed and four injured during a separate clash at Rodeni Cross.In Lasbela on September 12, the group claimed an attack on a military bomb-disposal convoy destroyed two vehicles and damaged two others, killing nine personnel and injuring more than 11.The BLA also claimed that 25 members of an alleged 'death squad' were killed in Killa Abdullah on September 13, followed by a four-hour clash involving Pakistani forces and the militants. Five BLA fighters were also reported killed.The group said 10 of its BLA militants were killed during the operations and vowed that its “military confrontation will continue on every front”, until Pakistani forces withdraw and an independent Balochistan is established.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Russia seizes assets of French firms, summons UK envoy over Ukraine support
articles.summary: Kremlin calls UK’s support for Ukraine an endorsement of ‘terrorism’ after recent escalation in weapons supply.
articles.body:
Russia has stepped up pressure on Ukraine’s allies, summoning Britain’s top diplomat in Moscow over arms shipments to Kyiv and seizing Russian assets of several Western firms.

The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned Britain’s charge d’affairs, Danae Dholakia, on Friday, issuing a formal protest over the UK’s “further increase” in weapons to Ukraine.

“London is placing itself in the position of an accomplice to the bloody atrocities committed by the Kyiv regime, which can only be characterised as terrorism and war crimes,” the ministry said in a statement.

Britain has maintained its support for Ukraine and says it will stand “shoulder to shoulder” with Kyiv and will provide whatever military equipment it needs, saying just last month that it will share classified weapons information.

Moscow’s move comes the day after Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia might be preparing to launch hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries that support Ukraine, including Poland. He said that such attacks would be framed as accidental, with the intention of weakening NATO states’ resolve to invoke collective defence provisions in the event of an attack on one of its countries.

French President Emmanuel Macron said on Friday that the threat posed by Russia’s shadow operations was growing across Europe and that Moscow had targeted ⁠⁠France with hybrid attacks in the past few ⁠⁠weeks.

“The Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified,” he said after a meeting with French political leaders.

France’s interior minister had met regional prefects to step up “vigilance in response to the Russian hybrid attacks”, Macron said, adding that he had ordered “the government to prepare a plan to protect our critical infrastructure” and the “most sensitive” defence industry and technology sites against drone and cyber-attacks.

As Russia steps up pressure on Ukraine’s political allies, it is also targeting Western companies.

Moscow has ordered the seizure of Russian businesses and assets of Swiss food giant Nestle and three French firms: retailer Auchan, DIY chain Lemana Pro (formerly Leroy Merlin) and logistics firm FM Logistics.

President Vladimir Putin signed a decree late on Thursday that changed the firms’ Russian operations to a new entity, LEV Management, which is managed by a Russian Ministry of Interior general, according to Novaya Gazeta Europe.

Nestle said it was still “assessing” the situation and its options but it remains “committed to taking all necessary steps to protect its rights”.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Friday that one of the reasons behind the decision was because Nestle and Auchan are companies from “unfriendly” countries.

Their assets are only under “temporary administration” and that no decisions have been taken as of yet, Peskov added.

Overnight Russian strikes hit multiple regions in Ukraine, sparking several fires across the country, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is to host the inaugural Carpathian Eight summit of several European countries.

They include Romania, Poland, Slovakia, Czech Republic, Austria, Hungary and Serbia, with the European Union also set to discuss regional cooperation.

Hungary and Slovakia have refused to send Kyiv direct military assistance in the past, though Poland and Romania remain staunch allies.

articles.title: Oregon man accused of killing five Portland-area women faces new charge in sixth death
articles.summary: An Oregon man accused of killing five women and dumping their bodies in the Portland-area has been indicted in the death of a sixth.
articles.body: An Oregon man accused of killing five women and dumping their bodies in the Portland-area has been indicted in the death of a sixth. Jesse Lee Calhoun, 41, was indicted by a Multnomah County grand jury Wednesday on a charge of first-degree manslaughter in the death of Elizabeth ‘Libby’ Gibson, who died on or about November 18, 2022, prosecutors announced. Gibson was 32. Gibson’s body has not been found, the Multnomah County District Attorney’s office said in a statement. “We will not stop. We will do everything in our power to hold him accountable and see that justice is done for each and every one of these victims,” District Attorney Nathan Vasquez said. “We remain committed to these families for as long as it takes.” The DA’s office did not provide more details linking Calhoun to Gibson’s death and declined to comment further. But in the same release, Multnomah County Senior Deputy District Attorney Melissa Marrero called the scope of the investigation “enormous.” “And to the extent that individuals have been willing to come forward in the past and provide information to us, no matter how small, that information has led us to where we are here today,” she said. Calhoun was arrested in June 2023 on unrelated parole warrants before being indicted in four of the six deaths in 2024 and 2025. He has been charged with five counts of second-degree murder and four counts of abuse of a corpse. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges. A court-appointed attorney for Calhoun, Cameron Taylor, did not immediately return a request for comment. The bodies of the five other women, all in their twenties and thirties, were found in early 2023, sparking fears that a serial killer was on the loose in the city. Calhoun was serving a four-year sentence for a 2019 conviction on charges including assaulting a police officer, attempting to strangle a police dog, and burglary. He was released about a year early, in 2021, after his sentence was commuted for helping fight Oregon wildfires in 2020 under a prison firefighting program. Gov. Tina Kotek revoked his commutation in 2023 after authorities began investigating him in the deaths of the Portland-area women. Gibson’s siblings, in a statement released through the district attorney’s office, said they were “grateful that a definitive step toward justice is finally being taken for our sister, Libby.” “Libby was kind, creative, and silly. She welcomed everyone with love and acceptance,” they said. “Her future was tragically taken from her way too soon.” They asked for “privacy as we process this heartbreaking development and continue to honor Libby’s memory.” Calhoun is scheduled to be arraigned on the new indictment next week.

articles.title: Woman gives police officer a lift in Nissan Micra while chasing man
articles.summary: The suspect reverse-rammed a police car and crashed into parked cars while trying to escape.
articles.body:
A driver came to the aid of a police officer who was chasing a suspect on foot - telling him to "get in" after stopping her Nissan Micra and offering him a lift.

The officer had been pursuing Jacob Roberts, 25, who had reverse-rammed a police car twice and crashed into parked cars and a building while trying to escape.

Roberts sped away from officers who had smelled cannabis coming from his van, with the chase seeing him drive in an erratic manner, failing to stop at multiple junctions, mounting pavements and putting pedestrians at risk.

The driver helped PC Kerswell catch up to Roberts, who was arrested and later jailed for one year and two months for a number of driving offences.

While fleeing from police in his white van, Roberts had driven into a dead-end street in Abercwmboi, Rhondda Cynon Taf, where he ditched the car and tried to escape officers on foot.

Police bodycam footage captured the moment the officer then runs to a red Nissan Micra driven by an un-named female driver and tells her: "I need a lift."

As she gave chase the woman is heard asking the officer to direct her, saying: "Where to?"

The officer is seen jumping out of the car after spotting the suspect and takes out his taser and arrests him.

During a search officers found two cannabis cigarettes on him.

Roberts, from Mountain Ash, was jailed for one year and two months for dangerous driving and disqualified from driving for three years.

He was sentenced at Merthyr Tydfil Crown Court on 16 September, where he pleaded guilty to dangerous driving, driving whilst disqualified, driving without insurance, failure to stop after a road accident, criminal damage to property, and possession of controlled Class B drugs.

Kerswell said: "Roberts was already banned from driving when he committed these offences - he showed complete disregard for all other road users, including pedestrians.

"I hope it acts as a deterrent for others who think of driving dangerously.

"It's lucky that no one was seriously injured during this pursuit. We hope this sentence will give Roberts time to reflect on his actions."

articles.title: New Bolivian cat claws its way into species list: What we meow
articles.summary: Purrfectly new to science: the first new wild cat found in over a century proves that cats do have nine (secret) lives.
articles.body:
A new species of wildcat, discovered in Bolivia, has been formally identified after the accidental discovery of a lost kitten and nearly 10 years of painstaking research.

The Leopardus tilcayo, which local people in the Bolivian Yungas, a band of cloud forest which runs along the eastern slope of the Andes, were aware of, was previously thought to be related to other wildcats in the region.

A study published in Current Biology this week has announced the first new cat species to be discovered in more than 100 years. The last was the pampas cat, reported in 1923.

Scientists have named the new cat Leopardus tilcayo, after the local Bolivian name for the animal.

The Leopardus tilcayo has been found living in the Bolivian Yungas, a band of cloud forest which runs along the eastern slope of the Andes, forming a transitional zone between the high mountains and the Amazon basin. This is a rugged, humid and largely under-studied ecoregion, which spreads into Peru and northern Argentina, although so far the tilcayo has only been genetically confirmed in Bolivia.

Researchers don’t yet know whether the species is confined to a single pocket of this forest or spread more widely across it.

Jonas Lescroart, a researcher at the University of Antwerp and coauthor of the study, said such a discovery is rare for the cat family. New species are sometimes “declared” when older scientific names are reinstated after genetic research shows a population was wrongly grouped with another species. That happened with the clouded tiger cat two years ago and the southern tiger cat, Leopardus guttulus, in 2013.

“It had never been given a scientific name, and it had never been formally described in a scientific way that was published,” Lescroart told Al Jazeera. “So we had the honour of coming up with a name for this animal and doing the formal scientific description.”

A local man found a kitten alone near the forest and, mistaking it for a stray domestic cat, brought it home to care for it. It lived with his family for about a year until 2016 when its wild instincts became impossible to ignore, and it started chasing the neighbours’ chickens.

Once the family could no longer manage the cat themselves, they surrendered it to Senda Verde, a refuge for animals. The refuge called in biologist and lead scientist of the Bolivian Felids Research Program, Paola Nogales Ascarrunz, telling her they had found a “weird cat”.

“Unfortunately, that’s the problem with the illegal wildlife trade,” Nogales Ascarrunz, told Al Jazeera. “When you want to pet a wild animal, then you think the power of love is going to change the behaviour of this animal. But a wild animal, it doesn’t matter if you give him the best food, it’s not going to behave.”

She added that this kind of case is common in Bolivia, particularly in the aftermath of wildfires, when orphaned young animals are captured and sold into the illegal pet trade before eventually being surrendered once new owners realise they can’t be kept.

When she went to see the for herself, she says she found an animal with a small, scrunched face, short round ears, long whiskers, and covered in leopard-like spots – but clearly too large and too wild to be a domestic cat.

Initially, she believed it was a Leopardus tigrinus, or tigrina, a small spotted cat found across much of Central and South America.

But, she says, something about the size and shape of the cat’s spots bothered her. It would take nearly a decade, a genetics collaboration spanning three countries, and DNA pulled from century-old museum skulls to prove she was right to be suspicious.

Perhaps leopards can’t change their spots but apparently, you can discover a new Leopardus with new spots altogether.

While Nogales Ascarrunz was puzzling over her “weird cat” in Bolivia, an entirely separate effort was under way to study tiger cats across the continent.

Lescroart and co-researchers in Belgium, Brazil, Bolivia, the United States, Colombia, the United Kingdom and Peru were busy collecting tiger cat DNA from across South America to resolve a long-standing taxonomic puzzle.

“The group of tiger cats has always been a contentious group with an uncertain taxonomy, and no one could really tell with certainty how many different species of tiger cats there were walking around,” Lescroart said.

By combining existing genomic data from northeast Brazil, Colombia and southern Brazil with new samples from the Guianas, Peru and Bolivia, the team built a far more complete picture of the group than had existed before, ultimately identifying five distinct species rather than the two to four previously expected.

Lescroart said the results were surprising. “When I started working on tiger cats, I was already aware from the start that, regardless of the results, something would have to be rearranged … but we would never have expected to find a completely undescribed species.”

Because tiger cats are what scientists call a “cryptic species” group, nearly identical in appearance but genetically distinct, the differences were essentially invisible without DNA analysis. “Physically, they are very similar and hard to tell apart at first instance,” Lescroart said, “and you need genetic research to dig down and find that there are important differences.”

“When we managed to put our data together, that is when the pieces clicked,” Lescroart said, “and we realised that the one in Bolivia is really a separate thing from the other tiger cats that we already had on our radar as suspected species or subspecies.”

The name, tilcayo, came from the people who live alongside it and who used the name for the animal to distinguish it from other small spotted cats in the region, such as Geoffroy’s cats and margays.

“It doesn’t have any meaning in Spanish, even Quechua,” Nogales Ascarrunz said. When the team asked local people where the name came from, “they would say things like ‘my grandpa told me’ or ‘my mother told me that’s the name of the cat’ – knowledge passed down with no accompanying origin story.”

Researchers do not know how many of them may exist. “We hope, thousands of them, but we have no idea,” Lescroart said.

They also do not know the cat’s full range within the Yungas, or whether the species extends into neighbouring Peru or Argentina.

Nogales Ascarrunz added that basic biology, including diet, predators and reproduction, is still undocumented.

Lescroart said the new species classification could change how tiger cats are protected.

Tiger cats are assessed collectively as “vulnerable” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List. But splitting one species into five means each newly recognised group covers a smaller population, which conservationists say could mean more of them need urgent, individual protection.

Genomic data adds to that concern: most tiger cat lineages show long-term declines, with some populations reduced by as much as 80 percent from historical highs, a trend that lines up with what Bolivian elders have told Nogales Ascarrunz: That they are seeing fewer and fewer tilcayos in the forest.

Paola Nogales Ascarrunz, who led the research that identified Leopardus tilcayo as a new species, observes the cat at the Senda Verde animal refuge in the Yungas region, in Bolivia, on September 1, 2026 [Fernando Faciole/National Geographic/Handout via Reuters]

articles.title: Stephanie Cole: Coronation Street and Doc Martin actress dies aged 84
articles.summary: She was best known for playing Dr Beatrice Mason in the 1980s BBC wartime TV drama Tenko.
articles.body:
Actress Stephanie Cole, known for roles in Tenko, Open All Hours and Coronation Street, has died aged 84.

A statement from her agent John Grant, issued on behalf of her family, confirmed the actress had been living with Alzheimer's for several years.

"Stephanie was an extraordinary talent whose long and distinguished career included many iconic performances in theatre and television," the statement read.

"She brought joy to millions through her many much-loved roles in sitcom and drama. She will also be remembered for her tireless work supporting mental health charities."

Solihull-born Cole, who trained at Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, after making her stage debut at the age of 17 – playing the 90-year-old medium Madame Arcati in Noel Coward's Blithe Spirit.

She went on to enjoy a lengthy career that spanned TV, radio and film and was perhaps best known for playing Dr Beatrice Mason in the 1980s BBC wartime TV drama Tenko.

The series chronicled the lives of British women in Singapore after the Japanese invasion and their consequent confinement in a Japanese prisoner of war camp.

Cole, in her breakout role, played a doctor who struggled to look after the women's health, opposite Ann Bell and Claire Oberman.

During this same period, Cole also played the moody customer Mrs Delphine Featherstone, aka "The Black Widow" in the Ronnie Barker-starring Open All Hours.

She would go on to win the award for best TV comedy actress for her part as the sharp-tongued photojournalist Diana Trent in Waiting For God.

But she cited her earlier performance as Muriel in Alan Bennett's monologue Soldiering On, as one of her proudest moments. The series also starred Maggie Smith and Julie Walters.

Her stage highlight, by her account, was in a West End production of A Passionate Woman.

Cole also played the aunt of Martin Clunes's titular character in the ITV medical drama Doc Martin.

Her other notable roles included Keeping Mum, and the BBC Radio 4 sitcom Cabin Pressure - alongside a fast-rising Benedict Cumberbatch - as Carolyn Knapp-Shappey.

"One of the joys of my character was how strong and feisty she is: she had the upper hand over the men, for the most part," she told the Guardian in 2018.

"Carolyn told it like it was and took no [rubbish]. We've all met women like her. She was very easy to put on, and I confess perhaps there's a little of her bossiness in me."

She also appeared in Coronation Street as Roy Cropper's mother Sylvia Goodwin, which won her another comedy prize, in her 70s, at the 2012 British Soap Awards.

Cole reprised her earlier role in the 2010s reboot Still Open All Hours, opposite David Jason, and also appeared alongside Suranne Jones in Gentleman Jack.

On Halloween 2018, she also guest starred in the live episode of Reece Shearsmith and Steve Pemberton's Inside No.9, titled Dead Line.

The actress's stage work included Driving Miss Daisy, Noises Off and King Lear.

In 2004, she returned to her debut theatre role in Blithe Spirit aged 63 when the play was revived at the West End's Savoy Theatre.

She also appeared in Midsomer Murders and Doctors. Her last major TV role was appearing opposite Greg Davies in his BBC comedy series The Cleaner in 2021.

Cole was married twice – first to playwright and theatrical fight director Henry Marshall, whom she divorced in 1988.

A decade later, she married fellow actor Peter Birrel, 30 years after the pair first appeared together in a production of Richard II at the Bristol Old Vic.

Birrel died in 2004. Cole is survived by a daughter from her first marriage, Emma Battcock.

Cole was made an OBE in 2005, for her services to drama, the elderly and mental health charities.

articles.title: Uber ordered to pay $40m to family of woman killed after driver left her on highway
articles.summary: The 23-year-old was returning home with a friend who got sick in the car when the Uber driver allegedly ordered them to get out of the vehicle on a California highway.
articles.body:
Uber has been ordered to pay $40m (£29m) to the family of a 23-year-old woman who was fatally struck on a California highway after the rideshare company's driver allegedly pulled over and ordered her out of the car.

Emily Normandin-Parker had booked an Uber for home with a friend on 12 August 2023, before her friend became sick and vomited in the car, court documents show.

Her parents said the driver pulled over to the side of the highway and forced the women, who were intoxicated, out of the car, after which Normandin-Parker was hit and killed by another vehicle.

Uber had argued that the driver was an independent contractor, and the company was not responsible for his actions.

"Emily did everything Uber tells riders to do - she made the responsible choice not to drive and we trusted Uber to get her home safely," her parents said in a statement about their daughter, a graduate of the University of California, Los Angeles. "That trust cost our daughter her life."

Judge Richard Stone ordered the rideshare company to pay the money to Normandin-Parker's parents after a five-day arbitration process, according to the law firm Panish, Shea, Ravipudi, which represented the family.

Arbitration is an alternative way to resolve disputes outside of court with a qualified arbitrator, in this case a retired judge.

Lawyers representing the family said that after leaving the women on the highway, the driver, Vu Tran, did not call for help for them. He instead pulled off to call Uber and demand they charge Normandin-Parker a cleaning fee, the lawyers said.

Tran showed "far more worry for his new car than he did for his passengers", Judge Stone said, adding that he could have taken the exit and dropped the women off at a safe location.

Uber said it believed the arbitrator was wrong in holding the company legally responsible for the event.

"We have continued to strengthen our approach to safety over the years, through new technology, policies and safeguards informed by safety experts, including additional guidance to drivers about avoiding drop-offs in unsafe locations," the company said in a statement.

The law firm representing the family said Uber had initially proposed a settlement that would give the parents $10m and require them not to speak about the incident, which they declined.

articles.title: Tier-2 cities see housing prices rise nearly twice as fast as top 8 markets: Report
articles.summary: News News: Residential prices across 11 emerging Tier-2 markets have grown nearly twice as fast as those in India’s top eight cities over the past decade, highli.
articles.body: Residential prices across 11 emerging Tier-2 markets have grown nearly twice as fast as those in India’s top eight cities over the past decade, highlighting the growing role of smaller cities in the next phase of India’s real estate expansion, according to a CII-Knight Frank India report released on Friday.The report, titled India’s Next Real Estate Markets, identified Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh Tricity, Goa, Indore, Jaipur, Kochi, Lucknow, Nagpur, Visakhapatnam and Coimbatore as emerging markets with the potential to drive the next phase of real estate growth.These 11 cities recorded an average residential price compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8 per cent between 2016 and 2026, compared with 4 per cent across the top eight markets, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Delhi-NCR, Hyderabad, Chennai, Pune, Ahmedabad and Kolkata.Smaller cities widen price growth leadThe gap has become more pronounced in recent years. Residential prices across the 11 emerging markets rose 63 per cent between 2021 and 2026, compared with 42 per cent growth across the top eight cities, according to the report.The average residential prices in the 11 emerging markets range from Rs 4,500 per sq ft to Rs 13,500 per sq ft.The report attributed the faster price growth to strengthening economic fundamentals, supported by infrastructure development, better connectivity and rising consumption.“India’s real estate growth is increasingly broadening beyond the traditional metropolitan centres,” Knight Frank India chairman and managing director Shishir Baijal said.Baijal said the investable opportunity in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, satellite markets and emerging corridors would depend not only on infrastructure creation but also on their ability to convert connectivity into sustained economic activity.He said cities that bring together employment, enterprise, population growth, consumption and urban capacity would be better placed to build deeper and more diversified real estate markets.Infrastructure, commercial activity support growthInfrastructure spending could provide further support to the expansion of smaller-city real estate markets.The share of infrastructure expenditure in total government capital expenditure increased to 55 per cent in FY26 from 39 per cent in FY15, the report said.The government’s three-year public-private partnership pipeline comprises 852 projects with a combined cost of Rs 17 lakh crore, according to the report.Commercial activity has also been expanding across smaller markets. Key Tier-2 cities recorded 11.2 million sq ft of warehousing lease transactions in 2025, with six of the identified emerging markets accounting for 5.3 million sq ft.Meanwhile, 24 Tier-2 cities accounted for 36 million sq ft of India’s total 134 million sq ft organised shopping-centre stock in 2025.The report estimated that India’s real estate sector could reach $5.8 trillion by 2047, with Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities expected to contribute 25-30 per cent, equivalent to $1.4-1.7 trillion.It said realising this opportunity would depend on the availability of serviced land, efficient approvals, reliable utilities and infrastructure capable of generating employment and enterprise.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: The St Helens man who revolutionised Hollywood sound
articles.summary: Pioneering sound engineer George Groves is honoured with a blue plaque at St Helens Theatre Royal.
articles.body:
Pioneering Hollywood sound engineer George Groves, dubbed 'the quiet little Englishman" by 1920s star Al Jonson, has been honoured with a blue plaque in the Merseyside town of his birth.

Born and raised in St Helens, the musician's definitive work in sound recording led him to collaborate with stars such as Judy Garland, James Cagney and Frank Sinatra, and won him a pair of Oscars.

Entertainment historian Mervyn Saunders, also from St Helens, called him "such a clever man".

This week, Groves, who was the leading recording engineer for Jonson in 1927's The Jazz Singer - one of the first 'talkie' feature films, was commemorated 125 years after his birth with a plaque inside the Theatre Royal.

Born in St Helens in 1901, young George showed an early talent for music, playing on stage at the Theatre Royal as a teenager.

He later attended the University of Liverpool, where he studied engineering and speech circuits.

He moved to New York in 1923, where he specialised in microphone technology, before relocating to Hollywood in 1927.

It was here he established his name, helping to develop talking movies, just as they were first sweeping the movie industry.

Saunders said Groves was involved in the early development of loudspeakers, as well as being responsible for evolving the radio microphone technology used today by theatres across the world to amplify performers' voices.

Given the role of director of sound at Warner Bros in 1957, Groves worked in the film industry for almost 50 years, until his retirement in 1972 - with 32 of his films receiving Academy Awards nominations.

He personally received two Oscars, the first in 1958, for Sayonara, the second in 1965, for My Fair Lady.

Other notable films he worked on included the 1968 Steve McQueen film, Bullitt, and Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf, with Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton..

He died in September 1976, in Hollywood, where he is buried.

Saunders, who was born down the road from St Helens Theatre Royal, organised for a blue plaque to be unveiled at the venue to mark 125 years since Groves' birth in the town.

The 80 year old said he had only learned about Groves' pioneering impact on film sound within the past decade.

"I thought, right, we've got to shout this man's credentials out a bit," he said.

The theatre is also celebrating its 125th birthday this year, having been rebuilt in 1901 following a fire.

Su Barton, a distant relation of Groves, unveiled the plaque at the theatre, where the young George once played the cornet on stage.

Coincidentally, Barton also studied sound engineering at university, so she was fascinated to discover George Groves was her grandmother's cousin while researching her family tree "many years ago".

"George was actually responsible for some of the course that I'd learnt," said Barton.

All sound was recorded at 78rpm "back in the day", she recalled, Groves "discovered that if you slowed the sound down to 33 and a third you could get voices to co-ordinate with mouths", which became a key component in the creation of the talking movie.

articles.title: Ex-Brookside star who fled after fraud trial arrested in Spain
articles.summary: Philip Foster was already serving a jail sentence for conspiracy to defraud, as of last year.
articles.body:
A former TV soap actor has been arrested in Spain after skipping bail before his trial for a £13.6 million fraud that conned would-be models.

Philip Foster, 51, who played Christian Wright in the Liverpool soap, is wanted and must serve an eight-and-a-half year jail sentence after being convicted of fraud and money laundering last year.

He ran an operation involving sham modelling agencies that exploited the dreams of aspiring young models and their parents for more than eight years.

The National Crime Agency (NCA) said that after jumping bail, Foster was convicted and sentenced in his absence at Sheffield Crown Court in February 2025 . He was arrested by officers on Thursday in Alicante.

Extradition proceedings to return him to the UK are now under way, the NCA said.

A National Trading Standards (NTS) investigation found that more than 6,000 victims parted with large sums of money on the false promise of securing paid modelling work in the fraud that Foster ran from his base in Marbella.

He used a network of associates in England to run a string of sham agencies and photography studios in cities including London, Manchester, Leeds, Bristol, Coventry and Nottingham which was uncovered after a six-year NTS investigation.

The victims were duped into thinking that a model agency was interested in them, with emails telling them they had potential after they responded to a local photographic studio and social media advertising campaign.

They were told they had to buy their portfolio photographs from the studio in order to join an agency and become an agency model.

Some of them used credit deals arranged by the fraudsters or expensive payday loans to make the upfront payment.

In return, the victims got poor quality digital photographs that stood no real chance of landing them professional jobs and most did not get paid modelling work.

Foster bought high-end watches and cars with his share of the proceeds while many victims told NTS investigators they had been left financially and emotionally devastated, and felt humiliated and betrayed.

articles.title: A developer planned to bulldoze this 1910 Oregon bungalow and divide its 1.04-acre lot; a preservationist bought it for $610,000 with only days to act, restored it and it has now sold for $1.47 million
articles.summary: US News: A historic 1910 Arts and Crafts bungalow in Lake Oswego that came within two days of being demolished by developers has sold for $1.47 million after a.
articles.body: A historic 1910 Arts and Crafts bungalow in Lake Oswego that came within two days of being demolished by developers has sold for $1.47 million after a major, multi-year restoration. Known locally as the Emma Austin House, the 3,074-square-foot home sits on a 1.04-acre wooded lot at 49 Briarwood Road in one of Oregon's most exclusive residential areas. The property was set to be demolished after a developer bought the land with plans to tear down the house, divide the tree-covered lot and build several high-density homes.Rescue within 48 hoursThe home was saved after historic preservation advocates made an urgent effort to protect it. According to project records from McCulloch Construction, the Lake Oswego Preservation Society learned that the historic bungalow was in immediate danger and contacted Portland preservationist and builder John McCulloch. The preservation group told McCulloch that someone had to buy the property directly from the developer within 48 hours. Otherwise, demolition permits would move forward and the house would be lost. McCulloch bought the property for $610,000, stopping the planned division of the land. The Lake Oswego Preservation Society later gave McCulloch its preservation award for stepping in to save the historic home. According to real estate records published in William J. Hawkins III's book Classic Houses of Portland, Oregon, 1850-1950, the bungalow is considered one of the region's best examples of early 20th-century Arts and Crafts design.Architect and originsEmma Austin, a wealthy Portland resident, commissioned the house in 1910. At the time, Lake Oswego was still known as "Sucker Lake" and was mainly a rural escape for people from the city. Austin hired well-known Portland architect Joseph Jacobberger to design the home. Jacobberger was known for his Craftsman and Arts and Crafts houses across the Pacific Northwest. He preferred natural materials instead of the heavy decoration common in Victorian homes. The house's design was influenced by the Greene and Greene style that became popular in California. It includes large stone columns, Japanese-inspired wooden framing and wide roof edges covered with rustic cedar shingles. Despite its historic design, the property did not have official city landmark status. This left its 1.04-acre lot open to possible redevelopment.Major restorationAfter buying the property, McCulloch Construction began a complete renovation from the studs out. The goal was to update the home's systems while keeping its original early-20th-century appearance. According to The Oregonian, workers replaced damaged stone details with matching river rock collected nearby. The same type of stone was used to build hundreds of feet of new retaining walls around the gardens. Contractors added a new concrete foundation around the house to meet modern earthquake safety codes. They also replaced the electrical and plumbing systems and installed more efficient heating and cooling equipment. Inside, workers removed layers of old paint and restored the original woodwork. McCulloch spent more than $75,000 on specialized interior painting and finishing. The team also found and restored light fixtures from the period to replace modern ones. The second floor was expanded to create a main bedroom suite with a private fireplace, marble finishes and heated bathroom floors. Workers also turned the low-ceiling basement into a full-height lower level with a climate-controlled custom wine cellar. Outside, the property still has mature rose gardens, a gazebo, an artificial fountain, a waterfall and coastal redwoods supplied by a natural stream running through the property.Successful resaleAfter the structural, mechanical and cosmetic work was finished, the house went on the market as a modern luxury home that combines historic architecture with updated features. Recent property records from Redfin and local MLS databases show that the estate sold for $1.47 million. The sale completed a multi-year effort to turn a home that was nearly demolished into a successful historic preservation project. In company project notes about the importance of saving historic buildings, McCulloch wrote: "Portland is changing so fast we are losing our sense of place and history. If you are torn between wanting to be close to everything and being touched by nature, this is the place."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about King Charles
articles.summary: Princess Diana's brother tells the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg that "we'll forget her soon enough" were "exactly" the words used by the then-Prince of Wales.
articles.body:
Princess Diana's brother has told the BBC exclusively that he is "telling the truth" about a phone call with King Charles in the days after his sister's death.

Earl Spencer claims in a new book the then-Prince of Wales said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

But in his first interview since, Earl Spencer said: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said."

Reacting to the rare statement from the Palace, Earl Spencer said: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"

Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".

In response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."

When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."

Buckingham Palace declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments.

The remarks may bring a renewed focus to the war of words between the Palace and the King's former brother-in-law.

In excerpts of his book published by the Daily Mail, Earl Spencer claims the phone call took place after he insisted Diana would not have wanted the young princes to walk in the procession.

In his BBC interview, he says the King "went ballistic" and "ranted for a while", accusing his family of not having an adequate sense of duty.

"And then he stopped and I thought, oh now, now he's gonna pull himself together and say something more appropriate," Earl Spencer said. "And then, he said, 'we'll forget her soon enough'."

He said he couldn't say exactly what went through his mind at that moment as he was "just so stunned", adding: "I just, after a stunned silence, I said, I cannot believe you just said that. And I hung up on him."

Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family.

In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner".

Earl Spencer recounts being alerted to the crash by a phone call from his sister Jane in the middle of the night at his home in Cape Town, South Africa.

A call from Charles was among those that followed, and he alleges: "Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated - like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time."

The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, created a volatile atmosphere in the country at the time, with the royals accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and seeming to be out of touch with the public mood.

Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's death at the age of 36.

Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do".

In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day.

The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg will be on BBC iPlayer on Sunday from 16:00 BST and on BBC One at 18:30 BST.

articles.title: More than 112,000 displaced by Yemen fighting; thousands flee to Djibouti
articles.summary: United Nations says 22 million people need humanitarian aid as conflict intensifies.
articles.body:
More than 112,000 people have been displaced in Yemen and close to 3,000 have fled the conflict to Djibouti, according to the United Nations, as fighting intensifies between the Iran-allied Houthis and Saudi-backed forces loyal to the internationally recognised government.

“Our resources are very, very, very limited and our stocks will be depleted very soon,” Abdusattor Esoev, mission chief in Yemen for the International Organization for Migration, told reporters on Friday.

Most of the more than 112,000 internally displaced people have been displaced over the last two weeks, mainly along the west coast and in the provinces of Taiz and Lahj, he added.

The displacement began when the Houthis made a rapid advance , seizing control of the entire Red Sea coast of Yemen to tighten their grip on the vital shipping route, the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

Esoev estimates 22 million Yemenis – or nearly half the population – are in urgent need of humanitarian aid.

More than 65,000 registered refugees and asylum seekers in Yemen, mainly from Somalia and Ethiopia, are also threatened.

The crisis is growing “by the hour”, warned Francesco Galtieri, a representative for the UN Population Fund (UNFPA), adding that thousands of women who have lost all their possessions are on the run with their children.

Galtieri estimates that 2,000 pregnant women are among the displaced and around 200 are expected to give birth shortly.

Around 3,000 Yemenis have fled Yemen by boat to Djibouti, the UN refugee agency said. The shortest route across the Bab al-Mandeb Strait is just over 25 kilometres.

The UNHCR reports that more than 2,400 people made the voyage in the past week – mostly women, children and older people.

The influx is adding pressure on Djibouti and population of about one million people. It already hosts around 36,000 refugees, most from Somalia and Ethiopia, said UNHCR representative Sandrine Desamours.

“While the number may sound small,” it must be seen in proportion to the population, she added.

The strategically important Bab al-Mandeb links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and has become an alternative shipping route as the United States’ war against Iran choked the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Angel mom pleads with her party to 'grow up' on immigration after newlywed son killed in truck crash
articles.summary: Elizabeth Carter, a lifelong Democrat, says she is ashamed of her party after an illegal immigrant truck driver killed her newlywed son and his wife.
articles.body: A lifelong Democrat whose newlywed son and daughter-in-law were killed in a crash involving an illegal immigrant truck driver is pleading with her party to change course on immigration, saying she is "ashamed" of how her party has handled the issue. "I was shocked and heartbroken to hear that the man responsible for our son and daughter-in-law's death, the driver of the 18-wheeler that they collided with, that he was a part of Biden's catch-and-release policy," angel mom Elizabeth Carter told "Hannity" Thursday. Carter's son, William Micah "Billy" Carter, 25, and his wife, Jennifer Lynn Lower Carter, 24, were killed in November 2025, when their Subaru struck a tractor-trailer that had jackknifed across both lanes of U.S. Highway 20 in Oregon. The couple had been married for just 16 days. WATCH: 'LIFELONG DEMOCRAT' ADMITS SHE IS ‘ASHAMED’ OF PARTY AFTER SON KILLED IN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRASH The truck's driver, Indian national Rajinder Kumar, was charged following the crash and has pleaded not guilty. Federal immigration authorities who later took him into custody say Kumar entered the U.S. illegally near Lukeville, Arizona, in November 2022 and was released by the Biden administration, pending immigration proceedings. He later received work authorization and a CDL issued in California, according to Houston's FOX 26. "If it weren't for that, our son and daughter-in-law would still be alive," Carter said, pinning blame on both federal and state policies that made the tragedy possible. The heartbroken mother's comments came after speaking on Capitol Hill on Tuesday, when she pleaded for lawmakers to make changes to immigration policies. ICE LAUNCHES CDL FRAUD TIPLINE AS DHS HIGHLIGHTS DEADLY CRASHES INVOLVING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS "[My son and daughter-in-law] lost the Russian roulette game our government is forcing them to play," she said. "We allowed 10 million people in under Biden. How is there a different suggestion as to how to process them other than the same way they came into the country, en masse, leaving?" "I have to say, as a lifelong Democrat, I am ashamed of what my party is doing." Carter's husband, Dennis, also voiced frustration Thursday, focusing his criticism on policies that allowed Kumar to obtain a CDL. "Just because someone is incompetent and can't do the job that they wanted to do, just because they got here, that doesn't mean, ‘Okay, they're here, we should give them a job that they can't do and just turn them loose on the road,’" he told "Hannity." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Dennis identified himself as a lifelong Republican and also offered a contrast to his wife's political background, saying their marriage demonstrates that political differences do not have to become personal divisions. "We have learned that the two parties can exist in the same household, and we actually get along," he said. Elizabeth agreed, saying the couple knows "how to disagree without tearing each other apart" and instead tries to better understand the issues on which they differ. Elizabeth also imparted a challenge to the Democratic Party during her appearance, pleading for them to "grow up" and start communicating with ICE at the state level.

articles.title: 5 explosive claims in new book by Princess Diana’s brother
articles.summary: Only short extracts from a book by Princess Diana’s brother, Earl Charles Spencer, have been published so far. But they have already sparked a firestorm for Britain’s royal family, dredging up painful memories of Diana’s unhappy marriage to King Charles III, and provoking a rare, forceful rebuke from Buckingham Palace.
articles.body: Only a few extracts from a new book by Princess Diana’s brother, Earl Charles Spencer, have published so far. But they have sparked a firestorm for Britain’s royal family, dredging up painful memories of Diana’s unhappy marriage to King Charles III, and provoking a rare, forceful rebuke from Buckingham Palace. “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” a palace spokesperson said in a statement. CNN has not seen the book “Swan Song” ahead of its publication, but a spokesperson for Penguin Random House has confirmed the passages quoted by the Daily Mail, which is exclusively publishing excerpts from the book, are accurate. These extracts contain several revelations about Charles and Diana’s marriage, as well as the then-Prince of Wales’ reaction to her death. Here’s what you need to know about the book before its release next week: Charles ‘giddily elated’ after Diana’s death Perhaps the most incendiary allegations in these extracts are Spencer’s memories of how Charles reacted to Diana’s death. He details that fraught night on August 31, 1997, tracing the moment from when news first emerged of Diana’s fatal car crash in Paris, his frequent phone calls with his sister Jane, to when he rang his former brother-in-law after learning Diana had died. In that call, Spencer says Charles “sounded giddily elated – like a lottery winner.” “Looking back now, I suspect the prince’s first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not,” Spencer claimed. ‘We’ll forget her soon enough’ During a later call between the two men, as they argued whether Princes William and Harry should walk behind their mother’s coffin at her funeral, Spencer says Charles unleashed “a stream of anger,” before briefly stopping. “I assumed the pause signaled an effort to bring himself under control, but then he unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death,” Spencer wrote. “‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough!’” Spencer wrote. “‘I can’t believe you just said that,’ I said flatly, before hanging up.” Charles and Diana’s unhappy marriage Spencer also details his perception of his sister’s unhappy relationship with the then-Prince of Wales, and even claims that Diana tried to break off the engagement after Charles had “shown next to no interest in her” at his brother Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s 21st birthday party. “Immediately after that evening of escalating heartbreak, Diana went to see my father,” Spencer wrote. “She told him she could not go through with marriage to a man who clearly did not love her.” Her father refused to allow Diana to break the engagement, Spencer said. That incident came shortly after Diana had found a bracelet Charles bought for his now-wife Queen Camilla, Spencer claimed. And on the day before their wedding, Charles told Diana “she needed to know that he was very happy to marry her, but he was not actually in love with her,” Spencer wrote, citing a story his sister had told a “close friend.” ‘Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?’ Just days after the couple’s engagement announcement, Spencer claims Charles squeezed Diana’s waist and said, “Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?” Diana, who suffered from bulimia, found that comment “devastating,” Spencer said. “She would later share with me that her waist shrank from 29 to 23½ inches between her engagement and her marriage,” Spencer wrote. Queen Elizabeth II offered to restore Diana’s HRH title On the day of Diana’s funeral, Queen Elizabeth II offered to restore the “HRH” title she had lost following her divorce to Charles, Spencer claimed. The letters, which stand for “His or Her Royal Highness,” are used to denote specific senior royals. The late Queen had declared a year before the tragedy that the HRH style would be taken away in the event of a divorce – as was the case for Diana and Sarah Ferguson following her divorce from then-Prince Andrew. Spencer said Diana was “dreadfully hurt” by the “petty and vindictive” removal of that title, and he decided to reject Elizabeth’s “well-meaning” offer as a “consolation prize.” “I felt that I knew in my bones how she would view this posthumous award,” he wrote, recalling a conversation he had with the Queen’s private secretary, Robert Fellowes. “That’s very kind of the Queen, of course. But what’s the point, Robert? Now? I mean – Diana’s dead.”

articles.title: Lasers to zap missiles? China's 6th gen J-36 jet hints at radical new weapon
articles.summary: International News: China may be exploring the use of high-energy laser weapons on its next-generation fighter aircraft to defend against incoming missiles, after a state.
articles.body: China may be exploring the use of high-energy laser weapons on its next-generation fighter aircraft to defend against incoming missiles, after a state-owned aviation institute showcased a fighter-specific laser tracking and aiming system at a defence exhibition in Beijing.The Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC) Beijing Precision Engineering Institute for Aircraft Industry displayed details of a “fighter aircraft laser-weapon tracking and aiming system” at the 14th China International Defence Electronics Exhibition, held from September 15 to 17.Social media posts from the exhibition showed that the system was listed as weighing less than 380 kg, although several key performance specifications were obscured.The display listed transmission power as “00kW”, which could indicate a power level of at least 100kW if the obscured character represents a single digit. Its dynamic tracking accuracy was shown as “ μrad (RMS)”, with the actual figure redacted.System displayed alongside J-36 imageThe promotional material paired the tracking system with an image of a large tailless aircraft that Chinese military aviation researcher Andreas Rupprecht identified as the J-36.The J-36 is the unofficial designation for a three-engined aircraft first seen flying over Chengdu in December 2024. It is widely believed to be a sixth-generation fighter under development by Chengdu Aircraft Corporation, part of state-owned AVIC.Rupprecht said the AVIC display represented the strongest public indication so far that China is developing such an airborne laser system.Mark Cazalet, editor-in-chief of international defence news organisation Warsight, also said the illustration appeared to depict the J-36. He said the aircraft “likely has sufficient space, weight and power” to accommodate a high-energy laser.“Lasers are in many ways easier to implement on larger aircraft than smaller aircraft,” he said, with larger platforms more likely to have the space, weight and power available for the systems.The technology could also potentially be adapted for other large aircraft, including bombers, transport aircraft and airborne early-warning platforms.What could an airborne laser do?Airborne lasers could potentially provide aircraft with another layer of protection against incoming missiles. Cazalet said their limited range would make them more suitable for attacking incoming missiles or damaging and dazzling their seekers than for conventional air-to-air combat.Lasers could burn through physical targets only at relatively short ranges, typically several kilometres, while optical sensors could potentially be damaged or dazzled from greater distances, he said.Cazalet said the development of Chinese systems capable of countering long-range missiles was “not altogether surprising”, given US efforts to develop or field weapons such as the AIM-174B, AIM-260 and AIM-424.However, he said questions remain over how such laser systems would perform in operational conditions.Key technical questions remainThe exhibition display does not establish that China has already integrated an operational laser weapon onto a fighter aircraft.One major uncertainty is what is included in the advertised 380 kg weight. Cazalet said the figure likely covered components such as the beam director, laser source and cooling system. However, the display did not clarify whether the figure applied only to the tracking and aiming system or to a complete laser weapon.It also did not disclose the system's electrical power requirements.There is currently no public evidence that the system has been installed on or flight-tested aboard a Chinese fighter aircraft.Developing an airborne laser is considerably more difficult than deploying one on the ground because the system must generate and manage large amounts of power while maintaining extremely precise aim from a rapidly moving and vibrating aircraft.China has pursued airborne laser technology beforeChina has previously shown interest in mounting laser systems on aircraft.PLA procurement notices in 2020 sought suppliers for an “airborne laser attack pod” and control software for a “laser attack platform”. A military programme affiliated with state broadcaster CCTV also said China had developed a prototype airborne laser, citing academic research into energy storage and power supply.In 2021, a Chinese study used flight data from a transport aircraft to simulate how an airborne laser could maintain accuracy despite aircraft movement and vibration.AVIC has also disclosed testing of other directed-energy tracking systems. A July report in China Aviation News, an AVIC publication, said researchers at the institute had built and field-tested one such system within a year.The report described a March 2024 trial in which the system maintained a lock on a drone despite clouds, birds and increasing distance. Later versions were reportedly tested on multiple platforms, although the report did not identify those platforms or establish a connection with the fighter-specific laser system displayed in Beijing.US experience shows the challengeThe United States has faced similar technical challenges in attempting to develop airborne laser weapons.The US Air Force's Self-protect High Energy Laser Demonstrator, or SHiELD, programme sought to demonstrate whether a pod-mounted laser could protect fighter aircraft from incoming air-to-air and surface-to-air missiles.In 2021, programme manager Jeff Heggemeier cited wind speeds, turbulence and rapid aircraft manoeuvres among the “hard problems” encountered during development.The programme concluded in 2024 without a laser pod being mounted on a fighter test bed.For China's sixth-generation aircraft, therefore, the Beijing exhibition offers an indication of the direction of development rather than proof of an operational airborne laser weapon. The displayed system suggests progress in precision tracking, but its integration, power requirements, range and ability to defeat real missiles remain publicly unconfirmed.

articles.body: This story is part of NBC Selected’s New & Notable column, where we highlight our favorite product launches. We will continuously update this article throughout the month with new releases we think you should know about. Footwear, apparel and accessories launches Rothy’s used almost a decade of customer feedback to design the third iteration of The Point flat, a customer favorite women’s shoe. It now has a sleeker silhouette due to its refined shape and lower V-shaped topline, and it’s more comfortable and supportive with the addition of Achilles cushioning and a redesigned heel — these features help prevent rubbing while keeping your feet in place, according to the brand. There’s extra cushioning throughout the rest of the shoe, too, plus better arch support from the insole and a roomier toe box. Hulken’s rolling tote is an NBC Selected staff-favorite product, and the brand just released a wheel-less bag. It has wide straps you can hold or put over your shoulder, and there’s a small internal pocket with a zipper that’s ideal for wallets, keys, phones and more. The bag is roomy and lightweight, too. Daphne, Paige DeSorbo’s loungewear brand, just came out with the Ribbed Collection, a suite of new styles for your fall. Pieces are made with soft, breathable, textured fabric that toes the line between stretchy and structured, letting you feel cozy while looking pulled together. The Ribbed Collection includes five styles: the En Route Turtleneck, Sky Cardigan, Jet Lag Pant, Elsewhere Tank and Layover Cardigan. More notable apparel and footwear launches Cupcakes by CAKES BodyHill House Home Meadow & Mount and Berkley Square CollectionsKizik New Freedom Hike BootLand’s End Clear Pocket ToteSpanx BoostUp RunClub Collection and Booty Boost Wide Leg PantThigh Society WhispAir Cooling UnderwearUgg Women’s Uptowner Collection: Uptowner Tall Boot, Uptowner Biker Boot and Uptowner Short Boot Tech launches The AirPods 5 have up to 1.5 times stronger noise cancellation compared to previous models, according to the brand, as well as dynamic head tracking and adaptive audio that automatically switches between active noise cancellation and transparency modes. The earbuds have an IP57 rating for dust, sweat, and water resistance. They also offer hands-free Siri access and real-time Live Translation, with up to 4 hours of battery life. You can buy the AirPods 5 with a standard or wireless charging case. NBC Selected senior editor Shalwah Evans tried out the AirPods 5 after receiving a pair from the brand and immediately noticed that the open earbuds fit more comfortably than previous models. “I feel like the opening of my ear canal is tiny and a lot of buds just don’t fit well, so I was pleasantly surprised that these pods with no rubber tip didn’t budge,” she says. “I also love how crisp the ambient sound is when ANC is turned off, which is a huge plus for when I’m walking my dog and need to be aware of my surroundings crossing busy streets.” Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro looks similar to the previous model, but it has the brand’s new A20 Pro chip and is built on a 2-nanometer process, along with a variable-aperture 48-megapixel main camera for better low-light and depth control. There’s also a Max version of the phone. The biggest difference is screen size — the Pro has a 6.3-inch screen compared to the Max’s 6.9-inch screen — and battery life (24 hours versus 30, respectively). Additionally, Apple announced that it’s releasing its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo. Pre-orders start on October 16. Apple’s Series 12 Watch pairs a redesigned Health Sensing System and new S11 chip with much more frequent monitoring — think background heart rate readings every five seconds and HRV checks up to every five minutes, 60 times more often than the Series 11, according to the brand. All of this is analyzed to provide you with a new morning readiness score based on activity, vitals and sleep. There are also new AI features tied to the updated Siri, including Live Rewind, which replays the last 15 seconds of audio, and Siri Recap, which summarizes conversations the watch hears (you program this feature). The smartwatch comes in eight finishes, including two ceramic options. articles.title: In 2023, UCLA graduate was kicked out of her cab and was hit to death by another car. Three years later, Uber ordered to pay $40m to family
articles.summary: US News: Rideshare giant Uber and one of its drivers have been ordered by an arbitrator to pay $40 million in damages to the parents of a 23-year-old woman, Em.
articles.body: Rideshare giant Uber and one of its drivers have been ordered by an arbitrator to pay $40 million in damages to the parents of a 23-year-old woman, Emily Normandin-Parker, who was struck and killed by traffic after the cab driver kicked her and her friend out of the cab on a California freeway. The ruling, issued by retired California judge Richard A Stone acting as arbitrator, awarded $20 million each to the parents of Emily Normandin-Parker — Carol Normandin and Ken Parker — holding Uber and driver Vu Tran jointly and severally liable. An additional $300,000 was awarded to Normandin-Parker’s friend, Luna Moore.The 2023 incidentThe incident occurred on August 12, 2023, when Normandin-Parker was travelling home with Moore after a night out. During the ride, Moore became sick inside the vehicle. The driver, Vu Tran, pulled over at a freeway "gore point"— a triangular area where lanes diverge near an exit — on State Route 73 in Orange County.According to arbitration findings, Tran argued with Moore over a cleaning fee and ordered both women out of the vehicle in an unsafe area instead of taking a nearby exit onto MacArthur Boulevard to drop them off safely.After being left beside the highway, Normandin-Parker, who was intoxicated, wandered into traffic and was fatally struck by a passing vehicle as the rideshare car drove away. Arbitrator Stone noted that the driver "showed far more worry for his new car than he did for his passengers."Liability and rulingArbitrator Stone rejected the driver's argument that Normandin-Parker's entry into traffic lanes relieved him of responsibility. He also held Uber legally responsible, ruling that the company acts as a common carrier with a non-delegable duty of care towards its passengers. GPS evidence presented during the hearing revealed that after leaving the scene, the driver passed near Normandin-Parker’s body before exiting and contacting Uber to claim the cleaning fee.Uber disputed the arbitrator's legal findings in a public statement. "While we respect the arbitration process, we believe the arbitrator was wrong in holding Uber legally responsible for the tragic events of that night," the company stated, adding that its thoughts remain with the family. Uber confirmed that the driver no longer has access to its platform and noted that it has updated driver guidance regarding unsafe drop-off points.Lawyers for the family stated that Uber initially offered a settlement agreement following the arbitration decision that required strict confidentiality, backed by a $10 million penalty for each breach. The family rejected the offer."We turned it down because we would never accept that kind of condition. The case was never about money in the first place," said Ken Parker. The family has established the Emily Normandin-Parker Foundation to advocate for stronger safety protections for rideshare passengers.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire chairman after six decades
articles.summary: Since taking control in 1965, Buffett grew a struggling textile mill into a global conglomerate.
articles.body:
Warren Buffett has stepped down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, handing over leadership to his son Howard in the final chapter of a long-planned transition at the US business giant.

At 96, the world-famous investor will move into an advisory role as chairman emeritus and remain on the company board to offer his "judgement and perspective", according to a letter to shareholders .

The decision comes nine months after Buffett passed the chief executive role to Greg Abel, with his son, Howard, who has been a director since 1993, taking over non-executive board duties.

Known as the "Oracle of Omaha," Buffett built one of the most successful investment track records in modern history.

He took control of Berkshire Hathaway in 1965 when it was a struggling New England textile mill and turned it into a $1.1 trillion (£822b), global conglomerate.

Today, the business owns a wide range of well-known brands including GEICO car insurance, Dairy Queen, and BNSF railway system. It also owns large stakes in companies like Apple and Coca-Cola – a brand close to Buffett's heart, as he famously drinks five cans a day.

Buffett has made his mark through "value investing" – a strategy focused on finding companies with solid fundamentals , buying them at fair prices, and holding them for decades.

His annual letters to shareholders and festival-like annual meetings turned him into a leading mentor across the financial world .

Despite his retirement from the top board post, the change is considered an orderly passing of the baton rather than a sudden shock.

"The timing is right to complete the transition," Buffett wrote, noting he had recently celebrated his 96th birthday and the first birthday of one of his great-grandchildren, who is "moving a bit faster" than he is.

The company assured investors that day-to-day operations will remain steady.

While Greg Abel manages corporate strategy and capital decisions, Howard Buffett's main duty as chairman will be guarding the firm's "culture and values". A former farmer, philanthropist, and sheriff, the younger Buffett brings more than three decades of board experience to the role.

Buffett concluded his letter by saying it had been the "privilege of a lifetime" to serve as chairman, but acknowledged that in the end, "Father Time always wins".

articles.title: Iranians rally in biggest show of defiance against US since war began
articles.summary: Volunteers rallied through downtown Tehran to join campaign highlighting ‘self-sacrifice’ for Iran.
articles.body:
Hundreds of thousands of Iranians have marched in a government-organised show of defiance in Tehran, pledging their readiness to take up arms.

The Iranian government showcased a newly formed volunteer force at the rally on Friday. It will receive limited military and emergency response training to serve as an additional layer of security for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Basij militia.

Volunteers rallied through downtown Tehran in combat uniforms, some carrying flags and weapons, while the government displayed drones, anti-aircraft batteries and other weaponry.

Iranian authorities said 313,000 people joined the event in the capital. Attendance figures could not be independently verified.

Tehran’s IRGC chief, Hassan Hassanzadeh, told the state broadcaster IRIB that over 600,000 people had registered to participate in the voluntary Janfada-ye-Iran campaign. That roughly translates to “Those who sacrifice their lives for Iran”, with over one million expected to take part in the training.

Senior Iranian leaders at the rally included President Masoud Pezeshkian and Basij head, Hossein Taeb.

Taeb told participants that the volunteers would be ready for “full-fledged defence” and would be a “nightmare” for Iran’s enemies.

Iranian authorities say mobilising the new volunteer force is part of a broader defence strategy.

“The Islamic Republic has mobilised these people to show that they are united, that they have solidarity and that their people are ready to give anything for the country,” said Al Jazeera’s Sinem Koseoglu, reporting from the rally.

Women and teenagers have also registered with the volunteer units, she added.

“I want to show the world that Iran is strong and united. We don’t want war, but we’re ready to defend our country to the very end,” one of the volunteers, Bahera, told our reporter.

Another volunteer, wearing a combat uniform and carrying a rifle, said: “This is our homeland and we won’t let others decide its future”.

President Pezeshkian said in a speech that the rally was a show of solidarity, Koseoglu noted.

“This is not only a message to countries like the US and Israel, which are attacking Iran, but also to the Islamic Republic that we are ready for any crisis.”

Friday’s rally happened as the Iranian economy struggles under the US naval blockade of Iranian ports and new US sanctions.

Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, condemned the “brutal economic war, deliberately designed to inflict maximum pain and suffering on every Iranian citizen”.

As the latest addition to its economic pressure campaign, the US administration on Thursday went after digital currency networks that it says are illegally providing sanctioned Iranian entities with access to the international financial system.

The struggling economy was a key driver for protests last December that quickly turned into a challenge to the political system in place since the Islamic Revolution in 1979. Iran said about 3,000 people were killed in the protests, but activists say the state crackdown killed over 7,000.

However, the war launched in late February by US-Israeli strikes has since allowed the authorities to regain the initiative by presenting themselves as a bulwark against the country’s enemies.

The volunteer mobilisation campaign started in early April, at the height of US-Israeli attacks.

According to the authorities, more than 30 million people registered for a potential call-up, about a third of the population of 86 million.

articles.summary: Christian Castro pleaded not guilty to six federal charges tied to the shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis during a Minneapolis immigration operation.
articles.body: A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of lying to the FBI about a January shooting in Minneapolis pleaded not guilty Friday to six federal counts of making materially false statements. Christian Castro appeared in a federal courtroom in St. Paul after prosecutors accused him of shooting 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg through the front door of a Minneapolis home during Operation Metro Surge. Castro told investigators he was being attacked with a broom and shovel before opening fire, but prosecutors say surveillance footage contradicted his account. During his Friday court appearance, Castro, 52, was wearing an ankle monitor and was instructed by a judge to travel only between Minnesota and South Texas. If he has any altercation with law enforcement, he is required to report it within 72 hours, the judge said. He was then released. ICE OFFICER PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO LYING ABOUT MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING INVOLVING VENEZUELAN MAN Castro was previously held in Texas custody for about 90 days before he was released. He was held for so long partly because Texas Gov. Greg Abbott refused to sign an extradition warrant to hand him over to Minnesota authorities. Castro was booked in Minnesota last week following his release in Texas, his home state. Per his release there, Castro was required to wear an ankle monitor and to surrender his passport and firearms. He faces federal and state charges related to the shooting. ABBOTT TAUNTS FAR-LEFT AG WITH FIERY WARNING OVER ICE EXTRADITION FIGHT: 'SUCH BAD LAWYERS' Prosecutors said Castro lied about the circumstances of the shooting, which occurred during "Operation Metro Surge" — part of the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration. He said he was being attacked with a broom and shovel before he fired his weapon. The law enforcement operation saw thousands of federal agents in Minnesota that resulted in sweeping arrests, as well as the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens. ‘UNPRECEDENTED’: JUDGES REVEAL BEHIND-THE-SCENES COORDINATION ON TRUMP IMMIGRATION CASES CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Minnesota authorities have battled the Trump administration over who should handle any charges against Castro. The administration contends that only federal authorities have jurisdiction over the case. The Associated Press contributed to this report.
